title: Protecting a baby from RSV (monoclonal antibodies)
what: A guide for parents: your baby gets an injection of ready-made antibodies that protect against RSV, a virus that is dangerous for infants. It is not a vaccine, and protection starts right away.
why: For infants before or during RSV season, especially premature babies and babies with heart or lung disease.
duration: the injection takes a few seconds; with the check-up usually 15 to 40 minutes
tell_doctor: If your baby is sick now or has a fever
If the mother had an RSV vaccine during pregnancy
Allergies and reactions to past injections

prepare.title: Health
prepare.text: The doctor will examine your baby before the injection.

prepare.title: Timing
prepare.text: The injection is usually given before cold season, or soon after birth if it is already the season. Ask your pediatrician.

prepare.title: Feeding
prepare.text: You can feed your baby before the injection or right after. It calms the baby.

bring: A blanket and a bottle, or a place to breastfeed
steps: You hold your baby in your arms
The injection is given in the thigh
The injection is recorded in the documents
After the injection, stay at the clinic for about 30 minutes
feel: Your baby may cry for a bit
Sometimes redness at the injection site or a mild fever
after: Stay near the office for 30 minutes
Keep up the regular vaccinations on schedule
Protection lasts about one season. Ask your pediatrician
red_flags: Your baby has trouble breathing, a swollen face or a rash all over: call your local emergency number
Your baby is limp, refuses to feed or has blue lips: call your local emergency number

faq.q: How is this different from a vaccine?
faq.a: A vaccine teaches the body to make its own protection. Here, ready-made protection is given right away.

faq.q: Is it needed if the mother was vaccinated during pregnancy?
faq.a: Usually not. But the pediatrician decides.

reminders.text: Your baby's RSV injection is tomorrow. Bring the vaccination record.
